blogs.title: When Anaphylaxis Comes Back: Biphasic, Multiphasic, or Just Not Finished?
blogs.description: This post would unpack the diagnostic tension between biphasic anaphylaxis, multiphasic relapse, refractory anaphylaxis, and ongoing antigen absorption. Using this case, it would review why transient improvement after epinephrine does not always equal true resolution, and how these distinctions matter for monitoring, documentation, and escalation of care.

blogs.title: 0.3 mg Is Not 0.5 mg: Adult Epinephrine Dosing and the Hidden Cost of Convenience
blogs.description: This post would focus on epinephrine dosing in adult anaphylaxis, especially in heavier patients. The case highlights the practical appeal of auto-injectors in time-sensitive settings, but also the risk of underdosing when a 104 kg adult receives 0.3 mg instead of the guideline-supported 0.5 mg IM dose.

blogs.title: How Long Should You Watch Them? Disposition After Severe Anaphylaxis
blogs.description: This post would examine the persistent uncertainty around observation periods after apparent clinical resolution. It would discuss risk factors for recurrence, the limits of current prediction tools, and how clinicians can think through ward versus ICU placement when a patient initially improves but remains at nontrivial risk for relapse.

blogs.title: Repeat IM or Start an Infusion? Managing Recurrent Anaphylaxis at the Bedside
blogs.description: This post would explore the management dilemma raised by multiphasic anaphylaxis: continue treating each relapse with IM epinephrine, or transition early to a continuous IV epinephrine infusion. It would cover the tradeoffs in safety, monitoring requirements, nursing familiarity, and the absence of strong evidence to guide practice in these rare but high-stakes cases.

blogs.title: Steroids in Anaphylaxis: Tradition, Evidence Drift, and Why Practice Hasn’t Caught Up
blogs.description: This post would use the case’s mixed steroid administration to review why corticosteroids became routine in anaphylaxis, why that practice is now being challenged, and what contemporary evidence actually shows about biphasic reaction prevention. It would be particularly relevant for clinicians trying to reconcile older protocols with newer guideline recommendations.

blogs.title: Don’t Miss the Tryptase Window: Post-Anaphylaxis Testing and the Mast Cell Workup
blogs.description: This post would cover the laboratory and outpatient evaluation of atypical or severe anaphylaxis, including correct timing of acute and baseline tryptase sampling. It would then extend to the broader question raised by this case: when recurrent or unusually severe anaphylaxis should trigger evaluation for clonal mast cell disease such as systemic mastocytosis.
